content: Bowlegs, also known as genu varum, is a condition where the knees remain apart when a person stands with their feet and ankles together. This condition is considered normal in children under 18 months of age. Symptoms of Bowlegs: When standing with feet and ankles together, the knees do not touch. The bowing of the legs is symmetrical, meaning it occurs equally on both sides of the body. The condition persists beyond the age of 3 years. Causes of Bowlegs: Infants are born bowlegged due to their folded position in the uterus. As the child begins to walk and bear weight on their legs (typically between 12 to 18 months of age), the bowing usually starts to resolve. By around 3 years of age, most children can stand with their knees just touching while their ankles remain apart. If the bowing persists beyond this age, the child is considered bowlegged. Bowlegs can also result from certain medical conditions, including: Blount's disease (a growth disorder of the shinbone). Bone dysplasias (abnormal bone development). Improperly healed fractures. Lead or fluoride poisoning. Rickets, which is caused by a deficiency in vitamin D. Diagnosis: A physician can often diagnose bowlegs by visually examining the child. The distance between the knees is measured while the child lies on their back. Blood tests may be conducted to rule out rickets. X-rays may be necessary in the following situations: The child is 3 years old or older. The bowing is worsening over time. The bowing is asymmetrical (not the same on both sides). Other test results suggest an underlying disease. When to Seek Medical Attention: Contact a healthcare provider if the child’s bowlegs persist or worsen after the age of 3. Treatment Options: In most cases, no treatment is required unless the condition is severe. Regular follow-ups with a healthcare provider every 6 months are recommended. For severe cases or if the child has an associated condition, interventions such as special shoes, braces, or casts may be considered, although their effectiveness is uncertain. In some cases, surgery may be performed during adolescence to correct significant deformities. Prognosis: The outlook for bowlegs is generally positive, and most children experience no issues with walking. Potential Complications: Untreated or persistent bowlegs may lead to arthritis in the knees or hips over time. Prevention: There is no known way to prevent bowlegs, except by avoiding rickets. Ensure the child has adequate exposure to sunlight and consumes sufficient vitamin D in their diet.
